The Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog (Rana sierrae) exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with females attaining a considerably larger ultimate snout-vent length of 8.5 centimeters [Li = 8.5 centimeters] compared to males, which reach a maximum of 7.1 centimeters [Li = 7.1 centimeters]. This disparity in adult body size is likely linked to fecundity selection, as larger females can accommodate more eggs. The maximum reproductive rate for this species is estimated based on field observations of clutch size and frequency; at an average water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females deposit approximately 500 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 500 eggs per clutch] and typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a strategy that is common among high-elevation amphibians constrained by short growing seasons. This annual output represents a substantial energetic investment given the relatively low productivity of oligotrophic lakes.

Newly hatched larvae emerge at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.05 grams [Wwb = 0.05 grams]. This minimal initial mass reflects the endotrophic stage of early development, during which the tadpole relies entirely on yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The larval period is prolonged in the cold, oligotrophic waters typical of the Sierra Nevada, and metamorphosis occurs after approximately 912 days since birth  when reared at a constant temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. This exceptionally long developmental phase, spanning nearly three years, is an adaptation to the high-altitude environment where low temperatures dramatically slow growth and differentiation rates. During this time, the tadpoles feed primarily on periphytic algae and detritus, gradually accumulating the energy reserves necessary for the profound morphological transformation that accompanies metamorphosis.

Sexual maturation in Rana sierrae is a gradual process that occurs well after the transition to a terrestrial juvenile lifestyle. The age at which individuals attain puberty, measured from birth, is approximately 2190 days [tp = approximately 2190 days] when animals are maintained under the cold conditions of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. This extended pre-reproductive period, lasting six years, is among the longest recorded for any North American anuran and reflects the extreme constraints imposed by the short, cool summers of the alpine zone. The snout-vent length at which females typically reach puberty is 4.54 centimeters [Lp = 4.54 centimeters], while males become sexually mature at a slightly smaller body size of 4.45 centimeters [Lp = 4.45 centimeters]. This difference in size at maturation aligns with the species' overall pattern of female-biased sexual dimorphism.

Adult body mass also exhibits marked sexual dimorphism, reflecting the divergent reproductive strategies of each sex. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of 73.5 grams, more than 1.5 times the maximum recorded mass of males, which reach only 48.3 grams [Wwi = 48.3 grams]. This substantial difference is largely attributable to the energetic demands of egg production; gravid females carry large clutch masses that can represent a significant proportion of their total body weight. The species is relatively long-lived for a small anuran, with a maximum lifespan estimated at approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] when measured under the stable thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This longevity is consistent with a slow life-history strategy characterized by delayed maturation, low annual fecundity, and high adult survival.

Population declines of Rana sierrae across its historic range in the Sierra Nevada have been attributed to a combination of introduced predators, habitat alteration, and the fungal disease chytridiomycosis. The species' life-history traits, including its protracted larval period and delayed age at first reproduction, make it particularly vulnerable to these novel stressors. Adults are primarily aquatic or semi-aquatic, inhabiting lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams, where they forage on aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates. Breeding typically occurs soon after ice-out in early summer, with males calling from shallow water to attract females. The gelatinous egg masses are attached to submerged vegetation or rocks in lentic habitats. Conservation efforts focusing on habitat restoration and pathogen management remain critical for the persistence of this high-elevation endemic amphibian.
